_what: Two numbers separated by a hyphen or a slash beside a digital input are very often a sample-rate RANGE, not a bit depth and a rate. Written 2026-11-25 after Musical Fidelity's V90-DAC page.
_the_trap: Musical Fidelity's V90-DAC page lists « 1x RCA coaxial connector SPDIF 32-bit/192 kHz (16-24 bit stereo PCM) ». Read left to right that is a 32-bit input at 192 kHz. It is not. The same maker's MX-DAC page lists the same socket as « 2x RCA coaxial connector SPDIF 32-192kHz (16-24 bit stereo PCM) » - 32 kHz to 192 kHz, the range of rates the receiver locks to - and both pages then give the depth separately in the parenthesis, as 16 to 24 bits. The V90 page has simply inserted the word « bit » into the low end of a rate range.
_why_it_matters: `bits` would take 32 on a device whose own page says 16-24 in the very same line, and the consumer engine would be told it may send 32-bit integer audio to a socket that cannot carry it. Unlike most reading errors this one is contradicted on the same line, which is the only reason it was caught.
_how_to_tell: 32 kHz is the lowest rate S/PDIF receivers are specified for, so « 32 » at the LEFT of a rate pair is nearly always the bottom of a range. Three signs confirm it: the parenthesis gives a separate depth; a sibling product of the same maker writes the pair without the word bit; and a bit depth of 32 almost never appears on an INPUT, because the standard transports carry 16, 20 or 24. A real 32-bit figure on a converter page is normally the chip's internal width - the V90's « 32bit DAC circuit » - which is a property of the conversion, not of what the socket accepts.
_the_general_rule: A pair of numbers is a depth and a rate only when the page says so in words, or when the left number is 16, 20, 24 or 32 AND no separate depth appears anywhere near it. Otherwise read it as a range and record only the ceiling.
